propositions.text: I dismiss this appeal.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a citizen of Mexico.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and states the Appellant is a Mexican citizen.

propositions.text: The Appellant claims refugee protection as a woman subject to gender-based persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellant claims refugee protection as a member of a particular social group, being a woman subject to gender-based persecution.

propositions.text: She fears harm from her estranged husband if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: She fears that her estranged husband, XXXX, will harm her if she returns to her native Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims refugee protection as a woman fearing harm from her estranged husband in Mexico.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative in Merida, Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Merida, Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant has an IFA in Merida, Mexico.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues her estranged husband can locate and harm her in the IFA.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that her estranged husband will be able to locate and harm her in the IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues her estranged husband can find and harm her in the IFA.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in finding the Appellant has an IFA in Merida.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida, Mexico.

propositions.text: I find the RPD did not err and the Appellant has an IFA in Merida.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err. I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida, Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the key issue is if the RPD erred on IFA and concludes it did not; the Appellant has an IFA in Merida.

propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal and find the RPD was correct that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and agrees the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor needs protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant has been in Canada since 2008, married her estranged husband in 2016, and their daughter was born in Canada in 2017.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has been in Canada since XXXX 2008. She met her estranged husband, a Canadian citizen, in XXXX 2016 and married him in XXXX 2016. Their daughter was born in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant has lived in Canada since 2008, married in 2016, and has a daughter born in Canada in 2017.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified her husband had drinking and drug problems and was abusive; they split in 2017 when he returned to Quebec and she stayed in BC.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that her estranged husband had problems with drinking and drugs and that he became an abusive spouse. The couple split in XXXX 2017 when the husband returned to Quebec and the Appellant remained in British Columbia (BC).

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified her husband was abusive and they separated in 2017 when he moved to Quebec and she stayed in BC.

propositions.text: After the RPD decision, the Appellant filed for divorce in BC and seeks sole custody, child support, and spousal support.
propositions.quote: Subsequent to the RPD decision dated April 29, 2019, the Appellant filed for divorce in BC in XXXX 2019. The Appellant has asked the BC Court to grant her sole custody of her daughter, and to award child support and spousal support.

paragraphs.summary: After the RPD decision, the Appellant filed for divorce and seeks custody and support in BC courts.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified she was threatened by her estranged husband and his father, who has organized crime connections in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that she was threatened by her estranged husband and by his father who resides in Mexico and has connections to organized crime.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified she was threatened by her husband and his father with organized crime ties in Mexico.

propositions.text: The Appellant fears returning to Mexico because she believes her estranged husband would act on threats against her there.
propositions.quote: The Appellant says she is afraid to go back to Mexico because she believes that her estranged husband would act on threats against her if she was in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant fears returning to Mexico due to threats from her estranged husband.

propositions.text: The Minister intervenes asking the RAD to uphold the RPD decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Minister has intervened in this case asking that the RAD uphold the RPD decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister asks the RAD to uphold the RPD decision denying refugee status and protection to the Appellant.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the new evidence submitted by the Appellant should not be admitted as it does not meet Raza criteria.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that the new evidence submitted by the Appellant at perfection should not be admitted because it does not meet the criteria as set out in Raza.2

propositions.text: The Minister argues the new evidence is not material, relevant, and does not disprove unknown facts to the RPD.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that that the Appellant's new evidence is not material or relevant to the contested issues and does not disprove a fact that was not known to the RPD at the time of the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the Appellant's new evidence should be excluded as it fails Raza criteria and is not material or relevant.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the onus is on the Appellant to prove she lacks an IFA.
propositions.quote: The Minister further argues that the onus is on the Appellant to prove that she does not have an IFA.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the case law submitted by the Appellant is not relevant to this case.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that the case law submitted by the Appellant is not relevant to the present case.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues the Appellant must prove no IFA and that her case law is irrelevant.

propositions.text: I will consider the Minister's arguments in the following analysis.
propositions.quote: I will consider the Minister's arguments in the analysis that follows.

propositions.text: New evidence presented by the Appellant at perfection is accepted.
propositions.quote: NEW EVIDENCE Evidence presented by the Appellant at perfection is accepted

paragraphs.summary: The court will consider the Minister's arguments and accepts the Appellant's new evidence presented at perfection.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to introduce a letter from a BC lawyer and a Notice of Family Claim filed in BC Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: The Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. Letter from XXXX XXXX, Barrister and Solicitor, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. b. Notice of Family Claim filed in the Supreme Court of British Columbia on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks to introduce a lawyer's letter and a Notice of Family Claim as evidence.

propositions.text: Evidence can only be accepted if it arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been brought before the RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or, iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The law permits accepting evidence only if it arose after the RPD decision, was unavailable then, or could not reasonably have been brought before.

propositions.text: If evidence meets requirements, it must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: Evidence meeting requirements must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.

propositions.text: I find the new evidence arose after the RPD decision dated April 29, 2019.
propositions.quote: I find that the new evidence arose after the RPD decision dated April 29, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the new evidence arose after the RPD decision of April 29, 2019.

propositions.text: The new evidence is new, relevant, and credible as it provides information on the relationship and ability of the estranged husband to locate the Appellant and daughter in the IFA.
propositions.quote: I find that the evidence is new and relevant in that it provides additional information regarding the current relationship between the Appellant and her estranged husband. This information is credible in that it comes from a BC solicitor and barrister. The information is relevant to the determinative issue because it addresses the future ability of her estranged husband to locate the Appellant and their daughter in the IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the new evidence credible, relevant, and new, addressing the husband's ability to locate the Appellant and daughter in the IFA.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not requested a hearing under 110(6) of IRPA and the court will not convene a hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not requested a hearing under 110(6) of IRPA. I will not convene a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant has not requested a hearing under IRPA 110(6) and will not convene one.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to introduce four items into evidence in a July 16, 2020 submission.
propositions.quote: In a submission dated July 16, 2020, the Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. Response to Minister; b. A letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; c. An Application for child care benefits - special needs child; and, d. Paternity test results

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks to introduce four items into evidence in a July 16, 2020 submission.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to introduce a letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 in an August 31, 2020 submission.
propositions.quote: In a submission dated August 31, 2020, the Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. A letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXices

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks to introduce a letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 in an August 31, 2020 submission.

propositions.text: In deciding on late submissions or evidence, consider relevance, new evidence, and whether the document could have been provided earlier with reasonable effort.
propositions.quote: In deciding whether to allow an application for late submissions or late evidence, I must consider any relevant factors, including: a) the document's relevance and probative value; b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and, c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record

paragraphs.summary: The court states the rule for admitting late submissions or evidence, considering relevance, new evidence, and timing.

propositions.text: The Appellant's submission responding to the Minister's arguments on IFA is admitted.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant's submission in response to the Minister's submission is admitted to the extent that it provides the Appellant's response to the Minister's arguments with respect to the determinative issue of IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court admits the Appellant's submission responding to the Minister's arguments on IFA.

propositions.text: The Appellant's late documentary evidence is not admitted due to lack of detailed submission and explanation of relevance or new evidence.
propositions.quote: The documents submitted by the Appellant as late evidence are not admitted. The Appellant has not provided a detailed submission as required by the RAD Rules regarding the admissibility of the proposed documentary evidence: two letters from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, an application for childcare benefits, and paternity test results. The Appellant has not explained what new evidence these documents bring to the appeal and the relevance and probative value of the new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court refuses to admit the Appellant's late documentary evidence for lack of detailed submission and explanation.

propositions.text: Evidence exists about the Appellant's counselling and mental health support in Canada; new evidence on family law proceedings is allowed.
propositions.quote: There is evidence already before me regarding the counselling and mental health support that the Appellant has received in Canada. I have allowed new evidence submitted at perfection regarding the Appellant's family law proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes existing evidence on counselling and allows new evidence on family law proceedings.

propositions.text: The court's role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD decision was correct.

propositions.text: Sworn testimony before the IRB is presumed true unless rebutted; presumption does not extend to conclusions or assumptions.
propositions.quote: Sworn testimony before the Immigration and Refugee Board is presumed to be true unless the presumption of truth has been rebutted. The presumption of truth does not extend to conclusions or assumptions that a witness might put forward in testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites the rule that IRB sworn testimony is presumed true unless rebutted, excluding conclusions or assumptions.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida, Mexico, after hearing and submissions.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida, Mexico. The RPD canvassed Merida as an IFA at the RPD hearing and received post-hearing submissions from Appellant's Counsel and the Minister on this issue.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida after hearing and submissions.

propositions.text: The Appellant challenges the correctness of the RPD's IFA analysis.
propositions.quote: The Appellant challenges the correctness of the RPD's IFA analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant challenges the RPD's IFA analysis as incorrect.

propositions.text: IFA requires balance of probabilities that no serious persecution risk exists and it is reasonable to seek refuge there.
propositions.quote: The key concepts concerning IFA come from two cases. The adjudicating panel must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that: i. there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted or, on the balance of probabilities, subjected to a risk to life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the IFA and, ii. that conditions in that part of the country are such that it would be reasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for her to seek refuge there

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the legal test for IFA from two cases requiring no serious persecution risk and reasonableness to seek refuge.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in finding estranged husband and his father lacked means or motivation to pursue her in Merida and that it was reasonable to seek refuge there.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant's estranged husband or his father did not have the means or motivation to pursue her in Merida. The Appellant argues further that the RPD erred in finding that it was reasonable for the Appellant to seek refuge in Merida.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred on estranged husband's means and motivation and on reasonableness of seeking refuge in Merida.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD did not err and independently finds the Appellant has an IFA in Merida.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err. I have conducted my own independent analysis of the evidence and the testimony and I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error by the RPD and independently finds the Appellant has an IFA in Merida.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues estranged husband can locate her in Mexico due to Family Law proceedings initiated in BC Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that her estranged husband will now be able to locate her in Mexico because of Family Law proceedings that the Appellant has initiated in the Supreme Court of British Columbia (the BC Court). The Appellant has adduced new evidence that she has asked the BC Court to grant her a divorce, to award her sole custody of their daughter, and to order her estranged husband to make spousal support and child support payments to the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues estranged husband can locate her in Mexico due to BC Family Law proceedings she initiated.

propositions.text: The BC Court proceedings require document exchange; new evidence includes a letter from Family Law attorney about custody and contact likelihood.
propositions.quote: The BC Court proceedings will require that the Appellant and her estranged husband exchange documents before, during and after the resolution of the case. The Appellant introduced, as new evidence at the RAD, a letter from her Family Law attorney stating that it is rare for BC Courts to grant sole custody to a parent, and that it is likely that the Appellant will be required to maintain some level of contact with her estranged husband if they share custody of their child, Victoria, or if the BC Court grants her estranged husband visiting rights.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits new evidence that BC Court proceedings require document exchange and likely contact with estranged husband.

propositions.text: The BC Court will order support and access as appropriate, considering well-being; Appellant can raise concerns about husband's access.
propositions.quote: The BC Court will order such support and access as it deems appropriate in the circumstances of this action having due regard for the well-being of all parties. The Appellant will have the opportunity to bring to the attention of the BC Court any concerns she may have about her estranged husband's future access to their child and to herself.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes BC Court will order support and access considering well-being; Appellant can raise concerns about husband's access.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in its analysis of husband's ability to find her in Mexico given new evidence and developments.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's estranged husband's ability to find her in Mexico. Given subsequent developments in the case and the new evidence that the Appellant has adduced at the RAD, the RPD's analysis is no longer relevant. I find that, given the Family Law proceedings initiated by the Appellant, it is more likely than not that the Appellant's estranged husband will be able to locate her in Mexico in the future.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD erred on husband's ability to find her; the court finds husband likely can locate her in Mexico.

propositions.text: No evidence before the court that the Appellant's divorce petition has been decided by the BC Court.
propositions.quote: I have no evidence before me that the Appellant's petition for divorce has been decided by the BC Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no evidence that the Appellant's divorce petition has been decided by BC Court.

propositions.text: The RPD found estranged husband and his father lack means or will to contact and harm the Appellant in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant's estranged husband, or his father, would not have the means or the will to contact and harm the Appellant in Mexico.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues agents of persecution will have means to locate her in Mexico; court finds husband can locate her but risk requires both means and will to harm.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the agents of persecution will have the means to locate the Appellant in Mexico. Given the new evidence, I have found that the Appellant's estranged husband will be able to locate her in Mexico. In order for her to be at risk however, the agents of persecution must have both the means and the will to harm the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found husband and father lack means or will to harm; the Appellant argues agents have means; court finds risk requires both means and will.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by speculating that agents of persecution will not harm the Appellant.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in speculating that the agents of persecution will not be motivated to harm the Appellant.

propositions.text: Sanchez v. Canada supports that the RPD erred by speculating and making unsupported findings.
propositions.quote: The Appellant cites Sanchez v. Canada10 as a case, with similar facts to the present case, to support an argument that the RPD erred by speculating and reaching a finding not supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by speculating about persecution and cites Sanchez v. Canada to support this.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err and Sanchez v. Canada facts differ significantly from this case.
propositions.quote: I find the RPD did not err. I find that the facts in Sanchez v. Canada differ significantly from the facts in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not err and Sanchez v. Canada facts differ from this case.

propositions.text: In Sanchez, the family had property expropriated and the Federal Court found RPD's conclusion speculative.
propositions.quote: In Sanchez v. Canada, the family in question had already had their property expropriated by the criminals targeting them. The Federal Court found that it was speculative for the RPD to conclude the family would not be targeted further.

propositions.text: This case differs: Appellant suffered domestic abuse but no evidence of targeting by organized crime or further abuse after relationship ended.
propositions.quote: This is not the fact pattern in the present case. In the present case, the Appellant has suffered domestic abuse at the hands of her husband in the past, however there is no evidence that she has been targeted by organized criminal organizations or that she has suffered further physical abuse from her husband once their relationship ended.

paragraphs.summary: Sanchez involved property expropriation and speculative RPD findings; here, no evidence of organized crime targeting or further abuse after separation.

propositions.text: Appellant fears estranged husband's father due to suspected organized crime involvement but gave no evidence except observed behavior.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that she fears her estranged husband's father because she suspects his father is actively involved in organized crime in Mexico. The Appellant did not adduce any evidence of that involvement when asked by the RPD except that she had witnessed behaviour that she believed to be consistent with involvement with organized criminals.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant fears her estranged husband's father due to suspected organized crime involvement but provided no direct evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant called estranged husband's father to complain; he threatened to kill her if she reported husband to police.
propositions.quote: The Appellant stated in the narrative to her Basis of Claim form that she called her estranged husband's father, XXXX, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 to complain about her husband's behaviour. The Appellant testified that XXXX threatened to kill her if she reported XXXX to the police.

propositions.text: No evidence that the threat was intended other than to discourage reporting husband to police.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not adduced evidence or testimony that XXXX threat was intended other than to discourage the Appellant from reporting her estranged husband to police.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified about a threat from estranged husband's father to kill her if she reported husband, but no evidence of intent beyond discouragement.

propositions.text: RPD erred by not considering father's letter confirming ex-husband threatened Appellant and failed to assess its relevance and weight.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in not considering that her father provided a letter confirming that her ex-husband threatened her in 2017. The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to assess the relevance and weight of this evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by not considering her father's letter confirming threats by ex-husband.

propositions.text: RPD did not err in considering the letter; it referenced the letter in its decision.
propositions.quote: I find the RPD did not err in failing to consider the evidence. The RPD Decision specifically makes reference to this letter: The claimant states that in XXXX 2017 her estranged husband called her father in Leon, Mexico and told him that if the claimant returned to Mexico there would be problems for her and that he wanted access to their child.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not err as it referenced the father's letter in its decision.

propositions.text: The court has conducted its own analysis of the evidence.
propositions.quote: I have conducted my own analysis of this evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court has conducted its own analysis of the evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant's father affidavit recounts husband's call threatening problems if Appellant returned to Mexico with child.
propositions.quote: In an affidavit dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 that was before the RPD, the Appellant's father, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX states that, "one day in XXXX 2017 XXXX called me around 2:00 p.m. (Pacific time) to tell me that if XXXX went back to Mexico, there would be problems, because the son she was carrying in her belly also belonged to him..."

propositions.text: Father called Appellant after husband's call; she said husband threatened to take baby away and mentioned husband's father.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX states in his affidavit that when he called his daughter immediately after the call from her husband she said, "XXXX is threatening me that if I leave, he will take the baby away from me because it's his too, and we know who his father is."

propositions.text: Father feared retaliation from husband and his father and advised Appellant she is better protected in Canada.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX states, "Knowing the story of XXXX and XXXX, honestly, I was afraid they were going to retaliate against XXXX, then I said, you're right here the law is useless and there you are better protected."

paragraphs.summary: The father's affidavit recounts husband's threatening call, Appellant's fear of losing baby, and father's fear of retaliation advising Canada is safer.

propositions.text: Affidavit lacks detail on 'problems' threatened; no contact from husband or father since 2017 call.
propositions.quote: The affidavit offers no further detail concerning the "problems" her estranged husband told XXXX XXXX XXXX would arise if the Appellant returned to Mexico with their child. The Appellant told her father that she fears her estranged husband "will take the baby away from me because it's his too." XXXX XXXX XXXX does not elaborate why he fears retaliation from the Appellant's estranged husband and his father, and what form that retaliation might take. Neither the Appellant's estranged husband nor his father have contacted the Appellant's family in Mexico since the XXXX 2017 call.

paragraphs.summary: The affidavit lacks detail on threats; no contact from husband or father since 2017 call.

propositions.text: Appellant testified last contact from estranged husband was in 2018; husband believed to live in Quebec with another woman.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified at the RPD that her estranged husband contacted her last in XXXX 2018. The Appellant testified at the RPD that she believed her estranged husband was now living in Quebec with another woman.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified last contact from estranged husband was in 2018; he now lives in Quebec with another woman.

propositions.text: Appellant has not established credible evidence that estranged husband or his father have means and motivation to harm her in IFA.
propositions.quote: Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Appellant has not established through sufficient credible evidence that her estranged husband or his father have the means and motivation to harm her in the proposed IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant has not shown credible evidence that husband or father can harm her in the IFA.

propositions.text: The proposed IFA satisfies the first prong of the Rasaratnam test and is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The proposed IFA satisfies the first prong of the test set out in Rasaratnam. The IFA is Reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the proposed IFA satisfies the first prong of Rasaratnam and is reasonable.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding it reasonable for Appellant to relocate to Merida, ignoring services and her ability as single mother recovering from abuse.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that it is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Merida. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by not considering the services available to the Appellant in Merida and her ability to live in Merida as a single mother recovering from domestic abuse.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by finding relocation to Merida reasonable without considering services and her situation.

propositions.text: RPD fully considered reasonableness of IFA, including women's employment discrimination and improving situation in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The RPD fully canvassed the reasonableness of the IFA in its decision. The RPD considered that, while objective documentary evidence shows that women continue to face discrimination in employment in Mexico, Mexican law prohibits such discrimination. The RPD cited objective documentary evidence that the employment situation for women in Mexico is improving.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD fully considered the IFA's reasonableness, including women's employment discrimination and improvements.

propositions.text: RPD applied Thirunavukkarasu test requiring proof of adverse conditions jeopardizing claimant's life and safety in IFA; Appellant failed to prove this.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered the test set out in Thirunavukkarasu17 for what would make an IFA unreasonable. The RPD wrote, "The standard is high and requires proof that the adverse conditions that would jeopardise the life and safety of a claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location." The RPD found that the Appellant had not adduced the required proof of adverse conditions. I agree.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the RPD correctly applied the high standard test for IFA unreasonableness and found no proof of adverse conditions.

propositions.text: Independent review finds RPD did not err in finding Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida.
propositions.quote: I have conducted my own independent review of the testimony and the evidence before me. I find that the RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court independently finds the RPD did not err in finding a viable IFA in Merida.

propositions.text: Appellant receives better financial and social support and counselling in Canada than in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that she receives financial and social support services in Canada that she would not receive in Mexico. The Appellant receives counselling for psychological XXXX and has adduced letters from therapists attesting to her need for ongoing support and counselling.

propositions.text: RPD found some support services exist in Mexico but are not as good or accessible as in Canada; this does not make IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered that some support services are available in Mexico to women such as the Appellant, but the support services are not of similar quality to those in Canada or as easily accessible in Mexico as in Canada. The fact that the Appellant receives better support services in Canada than she would receive in Mexico does not make an IFA in Merida unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant receives better support and counselling in Canada; RPD found Mexican services exist but are inferior, not making IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Federal Court found returning to poverty with Canadian-born child does not give rise to refugee or protection claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD cited a case wherein the Federal Court found that it was not unreasonable for a Nigerian woman to return to possible poverty in Nigeria with a Canadian-born child. In that case, Mr. Justice Harrington wrote, "Ms. Sikiratu Iyile submits that it would be inhumane to send her back to Lagos, to return her to a life of begging and prostitution, particularly since she now has a Canadian-born daughter. However, that is a situation in which any young uneducated female might find herself in the big city. It does not give rise to a refugee claim or a claim for international protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act."

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Federal Court ruling that returning to poverty with Canadian-born child does not justify refugee or protection claim.

propositions.text: Appellant's family does not support her divorce decision for religious reasons.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has testified that her family does not support her decision to obtain a divorce from her abusive husband for religious reasons.

propositions.text: Appellant's father affidavit states family loves her and wants best for her.
propositions.quote: In an affidavit dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the Appellant's father indicates that the family loves the Appellant and wants what is best for her.

propositions.text: Evidence does not support finding Appellant would receive no help or support from family if she returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: I find that the evidence before me does not support a finding that the Appellant would not receive any help or support from her family if she were to return to Mexico.

propositions.text: The RPD considered the evidence before it.
propositions.quote: The RPD Considered the Evidence Before It

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant testified family opposes divorce for religious reasons; father's affidavit says family loves her; court finds evidence does not support no family support if returned.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by failing to consider Counsel's post-hearing submissions dated March 22, 2019.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in that it failed to consider the evidence before it, specifically Counsel's post-hearing submissions dated March 22, 2019.

propositions.text: I conducted an independent analysis and find that the RPD did not err.
propositions.quote: I have conducted my own independent analysis. I find that the RPD did not err.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD failed to consider post-hearing submissions; the court finds no error after independent analysis.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by not considering submissions on the level of protection the Appellant would receive in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in that it did not consider submissions on the level of protection that the Appellant would receive in Mexico.

propositions.text: I do not agree that the RPD erred in this regard.
propositions.quote: I do not agree.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD failed to consider protection level in Mexico; the court disagrees.

propositions.text: The RPD engaged with Counsel's submission about conditions in Mexico, noting high domestic and gender-based violence rates.
propositions.quote: The RPD engaged with the Appellant's Counsel's submission regarding conditions in Mexico in the RPD Decision. The RPD considered the evidence that Mexico has a high-rate of domestic violence and gender-based violence.

propositions.text: The Appellant's claim is based on fear of harm from husband and his father, not general gender-based persecution in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Appellant bases her claim on a fear of harm from her husband and his father. The Appellant does not base her claim on a fear of general gender-based persecution in Mexico.

propositions.text: The Appellant does not fit the profile for domestic violence victims in Mexico as she will not live with her estranged husband.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered that the Appellant does not fit the profile for victims of domestic violence in Mexico because she will not be living with her estranged husband.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD considered Counsel's submissions on Mexico's conditions and found the Appellant's claim specific and not fitting typical domestic violence profiles.

propositions.text: The RPD addressed an example of domestic violence in Merida, noting differences from the Appellant's circumstances.
propositions.quote: The RPD engaged in its decision with an example of domestic violence in Merida cited by Counsel in post-hearing submissions. The RPD noted that the circumstances in the example differed from those of the Appellant in that in the example, the abusing spouse was separated but not divorced and that he had been invited back into the family home.

propositions.text: In the example, police were responsive and detained the alleged perpetrator, unlike the Appellant's situation.
propositions.quote: The RPD also noted that in the example provided, the police in Merida were responsive to the domestic violence complaint and detained the alleged perpetrator.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD noted differences between a cited domestic violence example and the Appellant's situation, including police responsiveness.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err; the Appellant failed to meet the burden to refute state protection availability with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err. The Appellant has the burden of refuting the assumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. I find that the Appellant has not met this burden.

propositions.text: No evidence shows state protection would be unavailable to a Mexican woman assaulted by an estranged foreign spouse without right of abode.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence before me that state protection would not be available to a Mexican woman who was assaulted by an estranged spouse who was a foreign national with no right of abode in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not err and the Appellant failed to prove state protection would be unavailable in Mexico.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by not considering the Appellant's mental health issues and the viability of the proposed IFA city, citing Olalere v. Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in not considering the Appellant's mental health issues and the viability of the proposed IFA city. The Appellant cites Olalere v. Canada that the RPD must consider the psychological makeup of the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred by not considering mental health issues and IFA viability, citing Olalere v. Canada.

propositions.text: Olalere's facts differ significantly; no evidence shows the Appellant is psychologically unstable to risk in Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that the facts in Olalere differ significantly from the facts in the present case. The Minister submits that there is no evidence in the present case that the Appellant would be psychologically unstable to the point that it would put here at risk were she to return to Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues Olalere differs and no evidence shows the Appellant is psychologically unstable to risk in Mexico.

propositions.text: The RPD considered the Appellant's testimony about emotional wellbeing and support differences between Mexico and Canada.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err. In its decision, the RPD considered the Appellant's testimony that "she was not emotionally well enough to live and work in Mexico, and that she would not have access to the same type of supports as she would have in Canada."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD considered the Appellant's testimony about emotional wellbeing and support differences.

propositions.text: The three mental health documents do not support a psychiatric or mental health condition making the IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I have conducted my own analysis of the three documents the Appellant submitted in evidence regarding her mental health. I find that that the evidence does not support a finding that the Appellant suffers from a psychiatric or mental health condition, such that the IFA is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the mental health evidence does not support a condition making the IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: A detailed psychiatric report dated XXXX 2017 states no psychiatric diagnosis but notes significant psychosocial stressors and pregnancy.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submitted a detailed psychiatric report provided on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX signed by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXMD, FRCPC. Under the heading "Diagnoses" the report states: 1. No psychiatric diagnosis. 2. Significant psychosocial stressors including recent separation from an abusive partner, recently in Vancouver, social isolation, unsure of immigration status. 3. XXXX weeks' gestational age.

paragraphs.summary: A psychiatric report from 2017 states no diagnosis but notes psychosocial stressors and pregnancy.

propositions.text: The psychiatrist did not report any psychiatric disorders and recommended self-care with counselling and support.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX did not report any psychiatric disorders and she recommends self care combined with counselling and support.

paragraphs.summary: The psychiatrist reported no disorders and recommended self-care with counselling and support.

propositions.text: A registered clinical counsellor provided counselling to the Appellant and her then husband under BC Crime Victim Assistance Act in 2017.
propositions.quote: The Appellant provided a report from XXXX XXXX, a registered clinical counsellor who provided counselling to the Appellant and her then husband as part of assistance provided under the BC Crime Victim Assistance Act from XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, the date of the report.

paragraphs.summary: A clinical counsellor provided counselling to the Appellant and her then husband under BC Crime Victim Assistance Act in 2017.

propositions.text: The counsellor confirmed psychological and physical abuse but did not offer a diagnosis or mental health assessment.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX confirms that the Appellant suffered psychological and physical abuse from her estranged husband. XXXX XXXX XXXX recommended that the Appellant seek support from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX did not offer a diagnosis or mental health assessment of the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The counsellor confirmed abuse but did not provide a diagnosis or mental health assessment.

propositions.text: A letter from a XXXX at a Vancouver centre states the Appellant had stress and anxiety but could recover with support in Canada, not available in Mexico.
propositions.quote: In post-hearing submissions, the Appellant submitted a letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX a XXXX XXXX XXXX at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX) in Vancouver. XXXX XXXX XXXX states that that the Appellant was under a lot of stress and anxiety when she came to the Centre in XXXX 2018 due to difficulty supporting herself and her child and the emotional abuse that she has suffered. XXXX XXXX XXXX offered her opinion that the Appellant was strong and would be able to recover with the support available to her in Canada, but that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not think this support would not be available to the Appellant in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: A letter states the Appellant had stress and anxiety but could recover with Canadian support, which is unavailable in Mexico.

propositions.text: No evidence shows the letter's author has qualifications to provide expert opinion on the Appellant's mental health.
propositions.quote: I do not have any evidence before me that XXXX XXXX XXXX has the professional qualifications necessary to provide an expert opinion as to the Appellant's XXXX health.

propositions.text: The letter states stress and anxiety but offers no diagnosis or detailed mental health assessment.
propositions.quote: In any case, the letter simply states that the Appellant was under a lot of stress and anxiety and does not offer a diagnosis or detailed assessment of the Appellant's XXXX health.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence the letter's author is qualified and the letter lacks diagnosis or detailed assessment.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by not considering services available to the Appellant in Merida.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in that it did not consider the services available to the Appellant in Merida.

propositions.text: I do not agree; the RPD considered the services available in its decision.
propositions.quote: I do not agree and I find that the RPD did not err. The RPD considered the services available to the Appellant in its decision.

propositions.text: The RPD cited jurisprudence that better conditions in Canada than Mexico do not affect IFA reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The RPD cited jurisprudence to establish that the fact that the Appellant might be better off in Canada than in a safe place in Mexico is not a factor to consider in assessing the reasonableness of an IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD failed to consider services in Merida; the court finds the RPD did consider them and cited relevant jurisprudence.

propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee or protection status.
